    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, not long after fortifying their rotation with the signing of Trevor Rogers, the Chicago Cubs struck again by landing slugger Teruaki Soto out of Japan. The club confirmed the signing on Friday, and the contract is for $120 million over six years, ESPN reports.

    It has been revealed that earlier in the offseason, CBS Sports ranked Sato, who turns 28 in March, as the No. 4 free agent of the current 2026-27 class. Here's part of our write-up:.

    According to recent reports, "He will play the entire 2027 season at age 28 and is coming off a .306/.383/.609 slash line with 39 home runs, which won him Japan's first Triple Crown since Munetaka Murakami in 2022. Sato has a similar skill set but is not quite Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact challenges to slug 35 homers in only 127 games around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll.".

    Industry observers note that sato is expected to play a corner outfield spot for the Cubs even though he's a corner infielder by trade. He does, however, have significant time in the outfield, where the Cubs are in need of help after the incumbent corner outfielders, Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki, departed in free agency. In 2026, Suzuki and Happ combined for a WAR of 7.8, so the bar for Sato will be relatively high when it comes to replacing a chunk of that value.

    Sources indicate that in addition to the $120 million contract owed to Sato, the Cubs also must pay Sato's former team, the Hanshin Tigers, a posting fee. For contracts in excess of $50 million, the posting agreement between MLB and NPB mandates that the posting fee will be 20% of the first $25 million plus 17.5% of the next $25 million plus 15% of the total guaranteed value exceeding $50 million. In the Cubs' case, that comes to a bit more than $20 million they'll owe Hanshin.

    The Cubs are coming off a 2026 season in which they won 89 games and earned a postseason berth as the second-place team in the National League Central. In the playoffs, though, they were swept out of the Wild Card Series by the San Diego Padres in two games.

    Sons of LeBron James, Carmelo Anthony among notable college basketball players with family ties to NBA

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the best parts about Thanksgiving is reuniting with family, eating good food and watching sports.
    • Michigan State star Jeremy Fears Jr.
    • Recent findings suggest that if Fears is drafted in the first round this summer, he will join exclusive firm with his brother Jeremiah Fears, who was selected No.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the best parts about Thanksgiving is reuniting with family, eating good food and watching sports. Whether it's watching a massive NFC North showdown on CBS between the Lions and Bears or tuning into one of the best college basketball games of the week between No. 11 Michigan State and Arkansas, Thanksgiving will have something for everybody.

    Michigan State star Jeremy Fears Jr. was named Preseason Player of the Year by CBS Sports and has looked the part through the first three weeks of the season. Fears, who is the No. 35 ranked player on CBS Sports Prospect Rankings for the 2027 NBA Draft, is also improving his draft stock ahead of a wide-open draft with his play.

    Recent findings suggest that if Fears is drafted in the first round this summer, he will join exclusive firm with his brother Jeremiah Fears, who was selected No. 8 overall by the Pelicans in 2025. The Fears brothers could become the latest siblings to both get drafted in the first round of the NBA Draft if Jeremy is selected on the first day.

    Here is a list of siblings who were both drafted in the first round of the NBA Draft.

    Fears isn't the only notable sibling playing college basketball this season. Bryce James, the son of LeBron James, started the first three games of the season for Arizona. Kiyan Anthony, the son of NBA legend Carmelo Anthony, has been a key rotation piece for Syracuse this season. Andrej Stojaković, the son of one of the greatest shooters in NBA history (Peja Stojaković), has played like an All-American this season.

    Here are some of the most notable college basketball players playing this season with NBA bloodlines in their family.

    Basketball bloodline: Brother of Jeremiah Fears, who plays for the Pelicans.

    According to recent reports, the Fears brothers will have a chance to become the next set of brothers drafted in the first round of the NBA Draft. Jeremiah had a standout one-and-done season at Oklahoma before becoming a lottery pick. Jeremy redshirted during the 2023-24 season after being shot in the leg. Over the last three seasons, Jeremy has emerged as one of the best players in college basketball. He led the nation in assists last season and is on pace to do the same this season.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Peja Stojaković, former NBA All-Star who played for Kings, Pacers, Hornets and Raptors from 1998-2011.

    Andrej has a completely different skill set than his father, who lit up the NBA in the 2000s as one of the best 3-point shooters in the sport. Andrej is off to an incredible start to the 2026-27 season, highlighted by a 46-point outburst against Duke, in which 12 of his 14 field-goal makes came from inside the arc. Andrej is playing like an All-American this season and is helping Illinois maintain a top-ranked offense without David Mirković in the lineup.

    Basketball bloodlines: Son of LeBron James, NBA's all-time leading scorer who right now plays for 76ers, brother of Bronny James, who plays for the Lakers.

    The son of one of the most famous athletes on the planet began the season as a starter for Arizona while coach Tommy Lloyd was trying to build his rotation in the midst of the RJ Godfrey eligibility dilemma. James does have bragging rights over his older brother and father because he was part of the Wildcats' Final Four roster last season, something no one in his family had done before.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Gilbert Arenas, a three-time NBA All-Star during an NBA career that spanned from 2001-12 with the Warriors, Wizards, Magic and Grizzlies.

    After playing in 14 games last season, Arenas returned to USC for his sophomore season. It's looking like the right decision. Gilbert's son has developed into one of the best scorers in college basketball, averaging 21.3 points per game. Arenas has also boosted his draft stock tremendously and could be a lottery pick this summer.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Carmelo Anthony, a Syracuse legend who played for Nuggets, Knicks, Thunder, Rockets, Trail Blazers and Lakers from 2003-2022.

    In a recent development, after appearing in 29 games last season at his father's alma mater, Anthony decided to return to Syracuse for his sophomore season. Anthony is Syracuse's leading scorer (13.5 points per game) despite coming off the bench in all six games this season.

    Basketball bloodlines: Son of Carlos Boozer, who played for the Cavaliers, Jazz, Bulls and Lakers from 2002-15; brother of Cameron Boozer, a rookie for the Grizzlies after playing for the Blue Devils last season.

    With Cameron Boozer declaring for the NBA Draft, this season marked the first time Cayden didn't play on the same team as his brother. Boozer returned to Duke for his sophomore season instead of entering the transfer portal and has started five of his team's first six games this season and is averaging 6.2 points and 4.3 assists.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Scottie Pippen, a Naismith Hall-of-Famer after his 17-season NBA career with the Bulls, Rockets and Trail Blazers.

    Pippen is at his third school in three seasons after previous stops at Michigan and Cal. In six games at Ohio State, Pippen is averaging 11.5 points, which ranks third on the team. He finished last season as Cal's second-leading scorer before entering the transfer portal.

    Basketball bloodlines: Son of Jason Richardson who played for the Warriors, Bobcats, Suns, Magic and 76ers in 14 seasons in NBA; brother of Jase Richardson, who plays for the Magic.

    Richardson, who was the No. 28-ranked recruit in the 2026 recruiting cycle by 247Sports, has appeared in four games this season for the Crimson Tide. Richardson started the Crimson Tide's season opener against Sam Houston State, where he finished with four points in 15 minutes.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Andre Iguodala, a four-time NBA champion during his career with the 76ers, Nuggets, Warriors and Heat from 2004-23.

    Iguodala, who was a three-star recruit in the 2025 recruiting cycle by 247Sports, did not appear in a regular season game during his freshman year. However, the son of the former NBA Finals MVP has appeared in four games this season for the Bears.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Trevor Ariza, an 18-year NBA veteran who won an NBA championship with the 2008-09 Lakers.

    Ariza, who was a four-star recruit in the 2026 recruiting cycle by 247Sports, is currently playing his freshman season at Oregon. Ariza has made four appearances off the bench and is averaging 5.0 points per game.

    Basketball bloodline: Brother of DaRon Holmes II, who at the moment plays for the Nuggets.

    Recent findings suggest that holmes, the No. 36 player in the 2026 recruiting cycle by 247Sports, is looking like a key rotational piece for the Wildcats. The brother of the former first-round pick out of Dayton has made six appearances off the bench this season for the No. 8 Wildcats.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Dominique Wilkins, who is in the Naismith Hall of Fame after playing for the Hawks, Clippers, Celtics, Spurs during his long NBA career.

    According to recent reports, the son of one of the greatest dunkers in NBA history made 32 games off the bench for Georgia last season before transferring to play for the Golden Bears. He has started seven games this season for Cal.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Jermaine O'Neal Sr., who played in NBA from 1996-2014 for the Trail Blazers, Pacers and several other teams.

    Recent findings suggest that the son of the former six-time NBA All-Star is having a breakout season at SMU. After making 34 appearances last season, O'Neal has started all six of SMU's games this season and is averaging 12.3 points per game.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Hakeem Olajuwon, a Naismith Hall-of-Famer after playing for the Rockets and Raptors from 1984-2002.

    The former four-star recruit has been a key piece for coach Kyle Smith this season. Olajuwon has appeared in six games (four starts) and is averaging 7 points per game. Notably, his younger brother, Malik Olajuwon, committed to and signed with SMU to play next season.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Brandon Bass, who played in the NBA from 2005-17.

    It has been revealed that bass has made six appearances off the bench thus far during his freshman season at FSU. His best performance came in Florida State's first game, where he dropped 13 points against Florida A&M.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Mo Williams, who played in NBA for 13 seasons, winning an NBA title with the Cavaliers in 2016.

    Sources indicate that williams is playing his freshman season at the same place where his father is an assistant coach. The former four-star recruit has been a key rotation piece for Mark Pope this season and is averaging 7.2 points off the bench.

    Basketball bloodline: Twin brother of Cooper Flagg, who was the No. 1 pick in the NBA Draft after playing for Duke.

    The twin brother of the No. 1 pick in the 2025 NBA Draft had to wait an extra year to play college basketball. That's because Cooper reclassified to join Duke in time for the 2024-25 season, while his brother played his senior season in high school. After making 32 appearances last season for Maine, mostly off the bench, Ace has started seven games for the Black Bears and is averaging 6.4 points.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Penny Hardaway, a four-time All-Star during his 14-year NBA career.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Brandon Roy, the Rookie of the Year in 2006-07 while playing for the Trail Blazers before his NBA career ended after a season with the Timberwolves in 2012-13.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Richard Hamilton, who played for the Wizards, Pistons and Bulls from 1999-2013.

    Pressing Impossible: Amorim Loses to Hürzeler – MH

    📅 20 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 21.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League mit 0 Kommentaren.
    • According to recent reports, rúben Amorim’s Manchester United faced Hürzeler’s Brighton on Matchday 22.
    • It has been revealed that manchester United started in a nominal 3-2-4-1 formation, which transitioned into a classic 3-2-5 shape in possession and a 5-4-1 shape out of possession.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 21.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League mit 0 Kommentaren.

    According to recent reports, rúben Amorim’s Manchester United faced Hürzeler’s Brighton on Matchday 22. While Manchester United focused on creating a pressing system that was as difficult as possible to bypass, Brighton once again showcased their incredibly challenging vertical play. You can find the tactical analysis of the match here.

    It has been revealed that manchester United started in a nominal 3-2-4-1 formation, which transitioned into a classic 3-2-5 shape in possession and a 5-4-1 shape out of possession. Amorim initially placed particular emphasis on a pressing system that varied in height.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, Brighton began in a nominal 4-4-2 formation. In possession, Hürzeler’s trademark positional rotations, vertical runs, and decoy movements for effective vertical play were continuously on display. Accordingly, Brighton operated flexibly from a variety of shapes, such as 4-2-4, 3-1-4-2, 2-3-2-3, and more. This flexibility makes Brighton’s possession game almost impossible to define through formations alone.

    Manchester United initially operated out of a 5-4-1 shape with varying defensive heights. This approach made it challenging for the opposition to play through, as different build-up phases required distinct patterns and connections. United’s central midfielders in the four-man line marked Brighton’s double pivot, Ayari and Baleba, man-to-man. The goal was to gain optimal control of Brighton’s central build-up play and apply immediate pressure whenever Brighton played through the middle.

    However, Brighton controlled the game during the first 10 minutes. Their holding midfielders positioned themselves close to the backline, creating a large gap between Manchester United’s five-man defensive line and the four-man midfield. This space was then exploited with various runs. When facing high pressing, left-back Estupiñán moved asymmetrically into the left half-space behind United’s first pressing block. This movement utilized the moment when Amad stepped out to press one of Brighton’s center-backs after bypassing Zirkzee.

    Recent findings suggest that united failed to adjust their pressing to this build-up variation throughout the match. As a result, this same pattern played a key role in Brighton’s build-up to the goal that made it 1-3.

    It has been revealed that against Manchester United’s mid-block, Brighton’s strikers, Welbeck and João Pedro, alternated their runs into the large space between the lines, targeting the gaps. This repeatedly allowed Brighton to bypass United’s first pressing line.

    The 1-0 goal resulted from this setup, facilitated by a counter-movement. As striker Welbeck made a run into the space between the lines, he pulled his marker, De Ligt, a few steps out of the five-man backline. Simultaneously, winger Mitoma made a deep run into the space that opened up. De Ligt was caught in a dilemma between applying pressure and covering the depth. A long ball bypassed United’s entire pressing structure, leading to the goal.

    Recent findings suggest that another reason for Brighton’s dominance in the first 10 minutes lay in their defensive work. United built up in a very positionally structured 3-2-4-1(/-5) shape. Brighton countered with a 4-4-2 in their high press and a 5-4-1 in their mid-block. With Minteh marking Diogo Dalot man-to-man on the flank, the two different defensive shapes emerged depending on Dalot’s positioning. Brighton’s two strikers also pressed United’s center-backs, Maguire and Yoro, on that side, applying intense pressure on the ball carriers on United’s left.

    On the other side, winger Mitoma positioned himself centrally when De Ligt had possession, cutting off the passing lane to Amad, who was positioned in the half-space. If the ball was played to full-back Mazraoui, Mitoma shifted out from the center to press, creating a cover shadow into the center. This approach effectively prevented United from creating any significant attacking threat on that flank as well.

    Sources indicate that around the 10th minute, the game shifted, and Brighton’s dominance began to fade. This was due to several adjustments made by United. To reduce the pressure on the ball carrier on the left side, the highly press-resistant Bruno Fernandes started to drop deeper, while the full-backs pushed higher. The resulting 3-3-4 shape was difficult for Brighton to press, as full-back Veltman, or the half-space defender in the five-man backline, was pulled out, and the space in behind could be exploited by either full-back Dalot or striker Zirkzee. This led to more possession phases for United and fewer pressing phases from Brighton.

    Another adjustment United made came from their 5-4-1 mid-block. The half-space defenders, De Ligt and Yoro, became much more aggressive in stepping out from the five-man backline to defend against the strikers making runs into the large space between the lines. This prevented Brighton’s strikers from turning after bypassing the first pressing block. To defend long balls to Mitoma, Mazraoui prioritized covering the space behind the advancing De Ligt. As a result, Brighton struggled to exploit the space between the lines and couldn’t progress as effectively into depth from their own possession.

    Additionally, Manchester United no longer pressed situationally from a 5-4-1 in a high press but instead switched to man-marking, with Zirkzee following the goalkeeper. This created much more pressure on the ball carriers for Brighton. Brighton also faced difficulties because the 5-4-1 system is much harder to break down than man-marking in a high press. This became evident in the sequence leading to the penalty goal. United suddenly switched to man-marking and forced the ball loss that preceded the penalty. United deservedly equalized.

    In a recent development, after the 1-1, the game became more balanced. Brighton tried to break down the 5-4-1 mid-block, while United focused on their defensive game. When Manchester United switched to man-marking in the high press, Brighton continued to struggle and often lost possession. It is questionable why United didn’t press more boldly and high man-to-man during this phase to maintain better control of the game.

    From Brighton’s perspective, a situational, more extreme overload at the moment of transition into high pressing—such as in the central space just behind the first pressing block—could have been a possible solution to challenge United’s man-marking, putting them in a dilemma between applying pressure and defending 1v1 on the wings.

    In a recent development, in possession, Brighton’s players frequently adjusted their positioning with small movements, creating new passing lanes, changing passing angles, and occupying spaces that forced the opponent into pressing reactions. Below, I have outlined the main advantages of three of the most frequently used shapes by Brighton against United, as well as the necessary reactions from the opponent.

    Recent findings suggest that another factor that makes Brighton’s vertical play difficult to defend is the continuous variety of space-creating or counter-movement runs into depth. These consistently create dilemmas and positional problems for the defenders. Below, I have graphically illustrated some selected runs used against United:.

    Recent findings suggest that despite Brighton’s possession game, Manchester United was able to prevent significant goal-scoring opportunities initially. From their 5-4-1 structure, the center-backs repeatedly defended aggressively, stepping out. Additionally, after bypassing the four-man midfield, it would drop back into position. This “recovery defense” made it difficult for Brighton to develop effective build-up play and exploit opened spaces. Furthermore, United’s players were well-prepared for potential through balls. In particular, the full-backs consistently intercepted balls played behind the defensive line.

    Sources indicate that towards the end of the first half and into the second half, small (forced?) mistakes began to creep into United’s pressing. While the failure to step out with Ugarte in the man-marking high press in the 39th minute and the failure to step out with De Ligt in the space between the lines in the 38th minute went unpunished, the delayed step-out by Yoro led to Brighton’s deserved 1-2 at that point.

    Industry observers note that especially in the second half, Brighton adapted to the man-marking high press by having center-backs step inside, breaking free from the cover shadow, when pressing the goalkeeper. This allowed them to find the open player in build-up, and Brighton lost possession less frequently.

    It has been revealed that longer defensive phases in the mid-block for Manchester United followed. To break down this block, Brighton’s possession play became less positionally rigid. Much more frequently, certain zones were overloaded. In particular, the space between the lines and the half-spaces were repeatedly occupied by multiple players to create numerical superiority and apply pressure.

    Industry observers note that united, on the other hand, struggled to create any significant goal-scoring chances. The high press could have been more effective with a brief orientation from the player pressing the goalkeeper to position the inward-dropping center-back into a cover shadow. From the 5-4-1 mid-block, too few dangerous ball recoveries and transition situations were created.

    Even from their own possession, Manchester United created too few goal-scoring opportunities. When Amorim’s team did get chances, it was typically through a ball played behind the wide players of the five-man backline. At the moment the press was triggered (when Brighton stepped out to the outer center-back), the forward half-space player dropped deep, and the winger made a run in behind. However, the lack of other ways to break the press led to too much predictability in United’s possession play.

    It has been revealed that as a result, the second half became more one-sided, with Brighton repeatedly pressing and trying to put United’s press under pressure. This ultimately succeeded, leading to a deserved 3-1 victory for Hürzeler’s team.

    Recent findings suggest that amorim’s press, which was difficult to break down, was ultimately cracked by Hürzeler. It is questionable whether more frequent defensive pressing, alternating with situational man-marking high pressing, might have been a better approach against Brighton, in order to better tighten the space between the lines and the area behind the defense, making the game in depth more difficult. Despite a higher mid-block, Manchester United hardly created any dangerous transition situations. This is an area that needs improvement.

    Hürzeler’s team, on the other hand, once again played highly attractive possession football. Frequent positional rotations, shifts in formations, overloads, and space-creating runs make Brighton’s possession game very enjoyable to watch. For the opponent, these constant shifts in zones over an extended period are incredibly difficult to defend. It is very likely that we will see more teams adopting similar principles in possession in the future.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that while Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani was once again one of the top performers in all of baseball this past season, he was not up to his recent standards. His production at the plate slipped from the heights of his 2023-25 run, and on the mound, injuries to his right biceps and left knee limited him to just 85 ⅔ innings during the regular season and zero during his team's playoff run.

    It has been revealed that the wear and tear on the 32-year-old four-time MVP has led to some speculation that Ohtani's days as a two-way phenomenon might be numbered, especially since the same injuries that limited his pitching availability also probably compromised him at the plate. That, however, doesn't appear to be the case.

    "That's how I can best help the team, the role in which I can best put my strengths to use," Ohtani recently remarked in Japanese, as translated by the California Post, about his usage as both a pitcher and the Dodgers' primary DH.

    Industry observers note that the expectation is that Ohtani will continue pitching in 2027, but, as ever, with an eye on having him energized and at or near peak when the postseason arrives. To hear Ohtani tell it, this means a careful workload, yes, but it doesn't necessarily mean an uncommonly light workload.

    "I think it's not good to not pitch enough," Ohtani said, "but that it's risky to pitch too much.".

    Even with the looming specter of an owner-implemented lockout that shuts down the sport and forbids contact between teams and rostered MLB players like Ohtani, this offseason may serve as a better foundation for Ohtani than last offseason did. That's because the 2025-26 offseason was complicated by preparation for the World Baseball Classic. As such, Ohtani figures to be able to adhere more closely to his typical winter routine this time around.

    According to recent reports, after the lockout ends and team-player lines of communication are reopened, Ohtani and the Dodgers will know more about his pitching plan for 2027. He's made just 14 starts in back-to-back seasons -- in 2025 his workload was limited as he returned from major elbow surgery -- and didn't pitch at all in 2024. Perhaps the hope is to find a way back to 2023, when he made 23 starts in his final season with the Los Angeles Angels.

    Whatever the specifics, the two-way show appears poised to go on until further notice, and that's good news for Ohtani, the Dodgers, and fans everywhere.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the Upcoming York Knicks may have cut off contract extension talks with Karl-Anthony Towns before the season, but Towns is doing plenty of negotiating on his own behalf with his play. Towns has been extraordinary for a Knicks team that still hasn't found its top form after winning the title, but is trending that way with five straight wins to get to 11-6.

    It has been revealed that towns leads the league with 13.9 rebounds per game. It's not just his size; he is a technician on the glass with the way he gets into the body of his man to stop his forward momentum and then almost springs himself back toward the ball for a two-birds-with-one-stone maneuver.

    It has been revealed that meanwhile, Towns is averaging 21.8 of just about the most efficient points possible for a shooting massive man at 54% overall and 41.5% on five 3s a game. His 15 straight double-doubles to start the season are a Knicks record. It's unlikely that he'll reach Bill Walton's all-time mark of 34 straight double-doubles to start the 1976-77 season, but with the way he's playing, you can't rule anything out.

    In a recent development, towns now has 20 straight regular-season doubles dating back to last year, four times more than the next highest active streak (Victor Wembanyama currently has five straight). Towns gets to his 3s in every way. He pops. Stretches. His step-back is about the only thing not going for him at present, but it's a nasty weapon with how dangerous he is as a driver.

    In a recent development, it's tempting to think Towns should be firing off even more 3s, but he is so dialed in on his attack times and zones that it's best to just let him continue playing on balance. When Jalen Brunson is in, he steps back. When Brunson is out, he ramps up the scoring. He's become the best high-hub passer this side of Nikola Jokić; no dime is too ambitious for him, as he is into full anticipatory quarterbacking rather than waiting for things to show open, which marks the highest level of facilitation.

    Get it to Towns at the top and cut, and you've got a good chance for a bucket:.

    KAT continues to hoop, good cut from Landry pic.twitter.com/5FG2CAKkGg.

    According to recent reports, KAT with the beautiful assist to Josh Hart for an easy 2.Can you imagine how fun playing basketball with KAT must be? pic.twitter.com/5L9QwYR2N8.

    Industry observers note that watch here as the Knicks flank Towns with a pair of two-man screening actions on each side. The first one, on his right, doesn't yield anything. But like a quarterback, he keeps going through his progressions until a second source produces fruit.

    On a retrouvé le dilemme mortelle des Playoffs 2026 sur les actions autour de KAT le playmaker :Balle plein centre et deux jeux à deux de chaque côté.Ne switchez pas, et c'est un cut ouvert pour OG pic.twitter.com/TmIIB0yNfk.

    These cuts are open for the Knicks because Towns, first, has pulled the major man away from the basket, and even more when Brunson is on the court and the defense has to be so concerned with the two-man handoffs that the lid is completely lifted.

    From there, Towns is a triple threat, weaponized as both a passer (four assists a game and almost six more potential assists), screener (55 screen assists), and of course as a driver when he sees the open lane.

    Sources indicate that notice how Towns doesn't just put the ball on the floor right away. He is so tuned into the off-ball movement. I know I keep using the quarterback analogy, but it's really what it is. He has the mobility to tuck the ball and run himself, but his first priority is more often to wait for his receivers to open up. His feel for when, where and how to attack has become surgical.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Arizona Diamondbacks have acquired catcher and former No.
    • It has been revealed that davis, who was the first selection of the 2021 draft out of the University of Louisville, turned 27 in September.
    • Davis is arbitration-eligible this offseason and is under team control through the 2029 season.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Arizona Diamondbacks have acquired catcher and former No. 1 overall pick Henry Davis from the Pittsburgh Pirates in exchange for utility outfielder/infielder Tim Tawa, ESPN reports.

    It has been revealed that davis, who was the first selection of the 2021 draft out of the University of Louisville, turned 27 in September. With the Pirates, he essentially functioned as ace Paul Skenes' personal catcher, catching 31 of Skenes' 32 starts in 2026 and making just 54 other starts behind the plate. Offensively, Davis has never adapted to the highest level. In 958 career plate appearances spread over parts of four MLB seasons, Davis has slashed .178/.265/.300, which comes to an OPS+ of just 55.

    Davis is arbitration-eligible this offseason and is under team control through the 2029 season. In Arizona, he figures to back up starter Gabriel Moreno, the two-time Gold Glove winner who finished sixth in the National League MVP vote in 2026.

    In a recent development, as for Tawa, who turns 28 in April, he has a career OPS+ of 84 over parts of two seasons at the highest level. He's spent time at every defensive position except for catcher and shortstop.

    The Pirates, at 82-80 last season, are coming off their first winning campaign since 2018. The Diamondbacks won 86 games but missed the playoffs for a third straight year.

    Now for some trade grades for this one.

    It's a trade for a backup catcher, so it is what it is. Maybe Davis, as, again, a former top pick, still has some unrealized upside, but he's not especially young. He was a consensus top-100 prospect in the minors, and as a minor-leaguer, Davis had a slash line of .290/.407/.529 in 827 plate appearances on the farm. At this point, it's not likely Davis is going to reach a vastly higher plane at the plate, but it's worth a swing given how limited his role figures to be in Arizona.

    Sources indicate that tawa is a right-handed-hitting utility sort who can steal a base on occasion but has never played shortstop. He'll be on Don Kelly's bench somewhere in the reserve pecking order between Jake Mangum and Jared Triolo.

    He might get some run since Mangum and Triolo are both in line for occasional platoon-duty starts. Tawa might be vaguely useful, but cutting bait on Davis represents an organizational failure.

    Between a Lack of Stability and Connection Concerns

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 25.01.2025 in den Kategorien Europa League mit 0 Kommentaren.
    • In a recent development, tottenham Hotspur and TSG Hoffenheim disappoint on Thursday evening in Sinsheim, with Hoffenheim showing promising adjustments in the second half but still falling short.
    • Christian Ilzer and TSG Hoffenheim were under pressure on the penultimate matchday of the UEFA Europa League: Only a win would keep their theoretical chance of direct progression alive.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 25.01.2025 in den Kategorien Europa League mit 0 Kommentaren.

    In a recent development, tottenham Hotspur and TSG Hoffenheim disappoint on Thursday evening in Sinsheim, with Hoffenheim showing promising adjustments in the second half but still falling short. It was a match defined by approaches and ambivalence, as both teams displayed glimpses of potential but lacked the necessary consistency and presence. (MX).

    Christian Ilzer and TSG Hoffenheim were under pressure on the penultimate matchday of the UEFA Europa League: Only a win would keep their theoretical chance of direct progression alive. The Austrian coach opted for a 4-2-2-2 formation. Oliver Baumann performed as usual as the goalkeeper, with Akpoguma and Nsoki forming the center-back duo, flanked by Jurásek on the left and Kadeřábek on the right. The double pivot consisted of Stach and Becker, while Bischof – who will soon join FC Bayern – and Hložek were deployed in the half-spaces. Up front, Morstedt and Kramarić played as a dual-striker pair.

    Industry observers note that on the opposite side, there was also significant pressure on Ange Postecoglou and Tottenham. Domestically, the team was in a difficult situation, and in the Europa League, a win was necessary to keep their chances of progressing in their own hands for the following week. The Spurs lined up in a 4-3-3 formation, with Austin in goal. Dragusin and Davies formed the central defensive pairing, while Gray and Porro occupied the full-back roles. In midfield, Maddison, Bentancur, and the young Bergvall played as central figures. The attacking line consisted of Kulusevski, Richarlison, and Son.

    Hoffenheim’s 4-4-2 Pressing System.

    The Hoffenheim pressing structure without the ball was primarily based on a 4-4-2 formation, which Ilzer had successfully used in recent weeks and also in Graz for midfield pressing. In this formation, Bischof and Hložek played as wide players, while Moerstedt and Kramarić formed the first pressing line. The ball-near striker didn’t press the ball-carrying center-back directly, but rather in a looser manner. The main focus was on controlling the diagonal dribbles of Dragusin and Davies and blocking the diagonal passing lanes into the center. Additionally, the far-side striker often took on the task of marking Bentancur, the central defensive midfielder.

    It has been revealed that A key characteristic of Ilzer’s approach was also that the strikers often moved wide from their diagonal pressing movements, putting more pressure on the width and preventing backward passes more effectively. This approach indirectly highlighted how crucial compactness is for Ilzer’s system. Without tight distances between the lines, it was difficult for the strikers to press effectively and create double pressure. In situations where compactness was not ensured, such as in some midfield pressing moments, unfavorable 1v1 situations arose that significantly diminished the advantage of the system, as the player could directly engage in a 1v1 duel instead of a 1v2 situation with the pressing striker.

    The attempt to block diagonal movements by the pressing striker inevitably led to a drawback: Tottenham was increasingly forced to play wide. Here, Hoffenheim highlighted some ambivalence. Tottenham frequently positioned their full-backs in half-space, forcing Bischof and Hložek to track them. The issue, however, was that the width, which should have been covered by the outer midfielders in the 4-4-2 system, was insufficiently secured. This created patterns that became an increasing challenge for Hoffenheim.

    Tottenham’s Width-Based Strategy.

    Postecoglou likely recognized the importance of exploiting width in deeper spaces ahead of the match, aiming to establish patterns that would facilitate effective use of the width.

    Industry observers note that the half-space players in the 2-3-2-3 system, Bergvall and Maddison, made dynamic movements into the wider areas, made possible by Hoffenheim’s first pressing line. The goal was to create shorter connections for the center-backs to progress into the wide areas. Complementing this, the full-backs, Porro and Gray, deliberately positioned themselves to bind Hoffenheim’s wide players, Hložek and Becker, in the half-space, thereby providing more space and time for Tottenham’s wide players.

    It has been revealed that hoffenheim responded solidly, especially through clear handovers. The central midfielder, in this case, Becker, would situationally take over the full-back, allowing the wide player to shift into the wide areas. However, Maddison could have made more of the side pressing angle from Hložek in some situations. By turning directly forward, he could have bypassed the pressure from the first line and, alongside Son, created a 2v1 against Kadeřábek. This option, however, was rarely utilized.

    Son repeatedly dropped deeper, pulling Kadeřábek out of the defensive line, but this often led to a lack of consistent height occupation for Tottenham. As a result, many progression opportunities—especially down the left side—remained ineffective. Although Hoffenheim’s attempts to push the full-backs wide created space in the half-space, Porro did exploit these opportunities successfully in a few instances, but overall, he did so too rarely to create sustained attacking dynamics. Richarlison could also have moved into these spaces more frequently in the opening phase to strengthen the attacking rhythm.

    According to recent reports, in general, one positive aspect was the consistent use of layoff play on the right build-up side, with Porro tucking inside. Bergvall, who positioned himself wide, showed excellent awareness of the game situations under pressure from the opposition. He swiftly recognized that Stach was marking Porro loosely, which allowed Bergvall to frequently find Porro in the center. This situation was well exploited, leading to effective one-two patterns and significantly supporting the build-up structure on the right side.

    Tottenham’s Half-Space Positioning and Defensive Weaknesses.

    According to recent reports, A recurring pattern for Tottenham was the positioning of the half-space players. They often remained in their usual positions, staying in the half-space rather than fully occupying the width, but frequently aligning with Bentancur, which resulted in a 2-5-3 system. This setup was often accompanied by deeper, but wide, movements from Kulusevski and Son.

    Due to the binding of Hložek and Bischof by Tottenham’s half-space players, Hoffenheim found it difficult to transfer the ball into the wide areas in a ball-oriented manner. Instead, they were forced to play out through the full-backs, which revealed weaknesses in the ball-oriented shifting of their defensive line. This resulted in large gaps, which Tottenham sought to exploit through quick vertical movements, especially in the half-space. Bergvall in particular pushed forward several times, but tended to do so too quickly, making it difficult for Kulusevski to receive the ball in these patterns. Nsoki, however, defended man-to-man and was able to largely isolate Bergvall’s movements.

    According to recent reports, overall, Kulusevski struggled, particularly under the pressure exerted by Kramarić’s pressing, which intensified the pressure. Return passes to the defensive line were consistently denied. Kulusevski had noticeable difficulty, especially with his first touch, to escape these tight situations.

    According to recent reports, an additional factor was that Kulusevski was often forced to turn using his weaker foot. Combined with the double pressure from Hoffenheim, this led to significant challenges in ball control, making it difficult for him to find Bergvall diagonally in the half-space.

    2-0 and 50% Possession at Halftime.

    Sources indicate that by the end of the first half, Hoffenheim had only partially been able to capitalize on Tottenham’s initial struggles. What stood out most was that the characteristic pressing through the strikers became less frequent, as Bentancur shifted closer to the ball, increasingly binding the ball-near striker, which led to a noticeable decrease in the intensity of the overall pressing. This change allowed Tottenham to play more return passes and initiate fresh build-up attempts without being under constant pressure.

    Additionally, Son was regularly placed in 1v1 situations in the final third towards the end of the half, which naturally created dynamics—helped by some unfortunate defensive actions from Kadeřábek. Furthermore, Richarlison and Maddison often found space in the in-between lines. The large gaps in Hoffenheim’s 4-4-2 system offered Tottenham the opportunity to target these players and create additional dynamics in their offensive play.

    Recent findings suggest that despite the early lead and a 2-0 score before halftime, Tottenham had just over 50% possession against Hoffenheim by the end of the first half. This surprisingly low figure was partly due to the disjointed nature of the game: many ball losses and fouls characterized the match, with Hoffenheim particularly focusing on physical intensity in the half-space. Additionally, Tottenham indicated general problems with coordination and connections between players. Notably, the lack of ball flow was apparent: passes often went astray, and there were difficulties with the first touch— a crucial disadvantage, especially for a style of play that heavily relies on width and time advantages along the sidelines.

    Sources indicate that through the 2-5-3 (or 2-3-5 in the final third), Tottenham also revealed significant weaknesses in their counter-pressing. This was primarily due to ball losses occurring frequently in the wide areas, with surrounding players often moving away from the ball. As a result, there was a lack of necessary ball concentration near the ball, making an effective, pressing-oriented counter-pressing difficult to execute, forcing Tottenham to frequently fall back instead.

    In Hoffenheim’s build-up play under Ilzer in the first half, a clear game proposal was evident: instead of a short build-up, they focused almost entirely on long ball distribution.

    In principle, the team played out of a 2-3-5 formation, with Kadeřábek and Jurasec positioned more centrally in the second build-up line, but occasionally shifting wide. Stach operated centrally between them, while Becker frequently advanced from the back line and occasionally dropped into the intermediate spaces.

    Recent findings suggest that the extreme overload of the back line was closely linked to Max Moerstedt, who acted as the target player. The striker regularly drifted to the left side, positioning himself close to Porro in order to receive long balls. Around him, three players—usually Bischof, Kramarić, and another teammate—positioned themselves to ensure that the area around the ball was well occupied.

    According to recent reports, the central issue with this approach, however, was the overly tight positioning of the players around Moerstedt. The second balls often ended up in more distant zones (green zone), areas that Tottenham could access well from their 4-4-2/5-3-2 structure. Notably, the wide players Son and Kulusevski frequently shifted excellently into these spaces, leading to dangerous counter-attacking situations.

    Both goals conceded in the first half resulted from ball losses in these zones, which Hoffenheim failed to protect effectively. Tottenham’s quick transitions and precise vertical play made the problems with the long ball distribution clearly visible.

    In general, Moerstedt had a rather unsuccessful day with the long balls. While the balls were often played back towards Baumann intentionally, these passes frequently lacked precision. Additionally, both Porro and Drăgușin were extremely dominant in aerial duels on this occasion.

    In a recent development, sending Moerstedt into an aerial duel within a densely populated zone also assumes that the team maintains a certain depth behind the target player. However, Hoffenheim failed to establish this depth adequately, resulting in second balls rarely being secured in the deeper areas.

    Towards the end of the half, Hoffenheim shifted its strategic focus from long balls to short build-up plays, which were mainly initiated on the right side. Kadeřábek positioned himself increasingly wide, which proved effective, as his direct opponent Son, starting from a half-space position, had to cover a long pressing distance and often arrived too late. This allowed Kadeřábek to receive the ball.

    From there, Hoffenheim attempted to play swiftly into depth to Hložek or Becker. However, Tottenham effectively defended this option through consistent man-marking. Becker’s dropping movements were frequently neutralized by Maddison’s covering shadow in the half-space, while Stach was largely covered by Richarlison, limiting the connections into the center significantly.

    In a recent development, in the second half, Hoffenheim continued with this approach, but increasingly operated from a 2-3-4-1 formation, while Tottenham defended in a 4-1-4-1. The full-backs positioned themselves in extreme width early in the build-up phases to maximize the pressing distances of their direct opponents. This approach remained effective: With clean first touches, Hoffenheim occasionally managed to beat their opponents with dribbles.

    Sources indicate that the biggest difference from the first half lay in the subsequent movements from wide positions. Unlike in the first half, Hoffenheim refrained from structurally overloading the last line. The focus shifted towards deeper positioning to create diagonal passing options. This allowed Hoffenheim to either play directly behind Tottenham’s defensive line or use the space in between, where Hložek was frequently available for a pass.

    There were also frequent rotations, for example between Bischof and Becker, which created additional dynamism. Kramaric often dropped into the defensive midfield space, allowing for the resolution of the isolation of that space by Richarlison, as Tottenham didn’t follow these wide runs in their man-marking system. This allowed Kramaric to distribute the ball on several occasions.

    A positive aspect was that Akpoguma kept up with Kadeřábek’s wide movements, constantly offering a return pass option. Meanwhile, Stach often dropped deeper to cover space for counter-attacks—a lesson learned from the first half. Since Tottenham struggled to defend the width consistently, the pressing became deeper, and Hoffenheim’s pressure steadily increased.

    Although Hoffenheim almost completely stopped playing long balls, the wide fullbacks presented themselves as viable options for diagonal switches, which were frequently sought. Sometimes Bischof also dropped wide to be available for these passes. These passes were mostly successful, as they were played into open spaces rather than into congested areas. Moreover, the 2-3-4-1 formation allowed for much better access to second balls due to the increased midfield presence.

    Recent findings suggest that for Tottenham, however, it remained a similar game to the first half. They still faced significant problems with the opponent behind them and technical difficulties in their ball retention play. Solanke added a bit more depth in the forward position, while Moore displayed more dribbling strength on the left wing. Despite some good individual actions, the problem areas—particularly in the final third from the very static 2-3-5—were still largely unresolved. Hoffenheim, on the other hand, simply had a better ball possession structure and dominated the game with nearly 61% possession. The counter-pressing issues ultimately led to Hoffenheim’s 1-2 goal.

    Towards the end of the match, Ilzer switched to a 2-4-4 system with double-wide wingers, while Spurs also switched to a 4-1-4-1 formation, defending much wider. They tried to directly cut off the connection to the wide fullbacks, which they succeeded in doing effectively. Once they were bypassed, however, the fullbacks advanced well. The central players were now more tightly marked, following movements towards the ball. It wasn’t until Moore failed to notice Kadeřábek’s off-the-ball runs in the 88th minute that Hoffenheim managed to break free on the wing and score the 2-3 goal.

    Overall, Tottenham’s initially wider setup made the half-space more accessible, which Hoffenheim repeatedly attempted to exploit. However, Moerstedt and Kramaric found few solutions against Tottenham’s well-defending center-backs. Several of these situations led to relieving counter-attacks for Tottenham, which were also the most dangerous for them in the second half. Especially towards the end of the match, as Solanke and Lankshear pressed for ball recoveries, Tottenham could quickly play vertically forward after regaining possession. Maddison’s dribbling pace was also frequently on display in these moments. It was clear that the fact Tottenham was ahead and Hoffenheim needed to win played into their hands.

    The conclusion is ambivalent. Both teams are going through a difficult phase, which was reflected in the match—many fouls, turnovers, and long balls shaped the game. It was not a particularly convincing display from two teams that, in terms of personnel and concept, should be doing better. Both sides were often forced into wide areas or specific zones, which fragmented the combination play in the final third and lacked the necessary dynamism.

    However, there were still glimpses of solid, familiar approaches, particularly from Hoffenheim, though the team still lacks the presence and stability required to compete against stronger opponents. As Ilzer highlighted in the post-match press conference: “We’ve learned that we need to be more stable to get the right results. In duels man against man, we lacked something. Still, you can see we can play really good football. We ruin a good game for ourselves when we make such simple mistakes. It was too easy for the opponent.”.

    Industry observers note that postecoglou’s team also revealed deficiencies, especially in ball movement, presence in the final third, and intensity without the ball. Ultimately, the team that managed to relieve pressure better came out on top, while the other, had they played the second half like the first, might have seen a different outcome.

    #153536. Scoring each round of the Draymond Green vs. Eddie Johnson beef, which goes back further than you think

    Scoring each round of the Draymond Green vs. Eddie Johnson beef, which goes back further than you think

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4447 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The funniest thing about this Draymond Green vs.
    • According to recent reports, that doesn't mean he hasn't landed a few blows in this bout, which actually goes back further than you probably realize.
    • Sources indicate that green is a guy who lives on a lot of people's last nerve.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The funniest thing about this Draymond Green vs. Eddie Johnson beef -- which has the feel of a teenage drama you wish never would've started but also kind of don't want to end -- is that Johnson fully thinks he's winning. You can see it. Hear it. Feel it. He thinks he is cooking Green, just as he believes he would've done on the court. In both cases, he's hilariously wrong.

    According to recent reports, that doesn't mean he hasn't landed a few blows in this bout, which actually goes back further than you probably realize. Johnson, who played 17 years in the NBA and has served as the Suns' color analyst for the last 25 years, has been a pretty consistent critic of Green. He clearly doesn't care for him, and he's obviously not alone in that regard. Green is an irritant of the highest order, and -- though he also has a sort of oxymoronic humility to him --an arrogant one at that.

    Sources indicate that green is a guy who lives on a lot of people's last nerve. He probably cost the Warriors a championship in 2016 when he couldn't control his temper as LeBron James stepped over him. He basically told Kevin Durant to get lost, choked out Rudy Gobert, backhanded Jusuf Nurkic, and most infamously went full Kermit Washington on his then-teammate Jordan Poole with the training-camp haymaker heard 'round the NBA world in 2022.

    Sources indicate that in 2025, Johnson resurfaced that Poole incident, which is where this bout began in earnest, and thus where we will begin the round-by-round scoring. Let's get it on!

    It's 2025, and Poole, whose career has been turned upside down after the Draymond punch, is now playing for the New Orleans Pelicans, who are facing Johnson's Suns in late December. Poole's new teammate, Jose Alvarado, gets into a scuffle with Phoenix big man Mark Williams, throws a punch, and you can see Poole's pretty hilarious reaction in the background.

    Look at Jordan Poole’s face when Jose Alvarado punches Mark Williams 😂😂😂 pic.twitter.com/5Pva2MJFUH.

    Notice that Poole does not make a move toward backing up his teammate, which Green -- after making fun of Williams for getting beat up by a little guy like Alvarado -- calls out on his podcast.

    Industry observers note that GREEN: I tell you what: if I'm in a fight, though, and my teammates stand behind me and do this? Come on, man. We can't be doing that. ... David West used to always tell us, man, if something go on on the court, you go over there because you don't know what's going to happen. I ain't saying you got to go over there and fight, but you at least got to go stand, because you don't know what's going to happen.".

    Johnson hears this and responds on the app formerly known as Twitter with the following:.

    JOHNSON: So based on your rhetoric, the entire Warrior team should have jumped you when you punched a young Jordan Poole? Just asking?

    According to recent reports, this is an early knockdown for Johnson. Here Green is up on his code-and-honor high horse saying you can't ever let a teammate get swung on when he, in fact, swung on a teammate?

    It has been revealed that johnson is absolutely right. By Green's logic, the whole Warriors team should have piled onto Green when he flat-out attacked Poole. Note Stephen Curry's location before Green makes his way over to Poole in the video below. He's not far away, but you sure don't see him enter the picture when the fireworks start. Apparently, in Green's book of brotherhood, Curry is a coward.

    Sources indicate that bottom line, Green tries to throw a keyboard roundhouse and leaves himself fully exposed to an easy counter, which Johnson is all too happy to deliver. Green is too staggered by his own hypocrisy to respond. He sulks to his corner and wonders if he underestimated his opponent.

    Recent findings suggest that it's the opening week of the 2026-27 season, and Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg has just gone scorched earth on Luka Doncic for being a crybaby (true) who is deserving of zero respect (not true). Green backs his teammate. So do Steve Kerr and Curry, both of whom say Lendeborg simply has to back up his talk on the court.

    Sources indicate that but Johnson doesn't appreciate Lendeborg's mouth. He's a different-era dude who believes "rooks are not allowed to speak." That specific comment will be made later in the exchange, but Johnson more or less voices this position on SiriusXM NBA radio. Green catches wind, and the bell for round two dings.

    Recent findings suggest that GREEN: So for these clowns out there like Eddie Johnson talking about, 'He's a rookie. Shut up.' Like no, You shut up. Why? Because he's a rookie. Should he shut up? Why?

    JOHNSON: He's [Green] a veteran. Get your hands on a rookie that seems to be unleashed and has not done a damn thing yet. Nothing. Now, do I think the kid has talent? Yes. Do I think that he might be a surprise pick? Yes. But he hasn't done anything yet. And he shouldn't waste his energy on talking about a great player like Luka after the game, and they just got their butt kicked by 30 plus. Come on, man. If you're a veteran, you've got to stand up to him.

    In a recent development, JOHNSON: So [Draymond] want to call me a clown? Dude, I scored more points than you in two minutes than you've done most of your career. Now, granted, you won some titles, and you jumped on Steph's back, and that's fine. But [I] ain't no clown.

    OK! Now we're throwing real blows! That "jumped on Steph's back" is a Johnson favorite. He throws it from a lot of different angles, as we'll see throughout this fight. It's his bailout punch. The haymaker when he's getting beat.

    It catches Green just before the bell, but by then the round had already been decided. Green wins on grown-up logic. Lendeborg is a grown man. He's 23 years old and has fought his butt off to get where he is. Didn't play high school ball until his junior year. Went to junior college. Stayed in school six years. His mom is battling cancer. Enough with the "carry my bags and shut up, rookie" nonsense. It's 2026. That lawn you don't think anyone younger than you has a right to stand on died a long time ago.

    This is where most people think the fight started, when Kerr stated on a radio interview that Curry being out with an injury "really limits Draymond's impact offensively.".

    "When Steph goes out, it really limits Draymond's impact offensively. There's no question. We're trying to sort through that and figure it out."Steve Kerr on Draymond Green's offensive impact without Steph Curry | @WillardAndDibs pic.twitter.com/ZI1SgTlLp2.

    In a recent development, green has nothing to do with this. He hasn't remarked anything. Probably doesn't even know Kerr is on the radio. But Johnson hears Green's name and his ears perk up, and he can't help but piggyback on Kerr's comment with a jab at Green's perceived status as a Hall of Fame lock, which he clearly disagrees with. He posts the following:.

    JOHNSON: Name me a Potential Hall of Fame player that will have that statistical personal resume going into the Hall. Then you have players like Mark Aguirre, Tom Chambers, Shawn Marion, and Kevin Johnson not get in?

    Green sees the comment, and the slugfest is on.

    It has been revealed that GREEN: Hahaha you named a bunch of players not named Eddie 🤣🤣🤣. Making it me vs. them not changing your life Ed.

    JOHNSON: My life is good, Draymond. Thanks for checking🙏🏿 I named Aguirre, Chambers, Marion and KJ for a reason. Your defense and impact on winning are part of your case. So here's the individual basketball question. How do you weigh that against the individual résumés of those four guys who could actually carry a team if the star player they played with is injured? Check my resume, even I did that many times. I got more players for you if you want? Just doing my job bro as an analyst. Isn't that your main job now and basketball is only when Curry plays?

    In a recent development, GREEN: I checked your resume like you told me Eddie. After your first 4 years, you found a role of coming off the bench to add some bench scoring. That's a great ROLE! You retired with the most points scored to never be an All-Star. That right there would say to me that scoring isn't the only way to make an impact. I was also ready to applaud you for being a 2x all star but that was the Other Eddie Johnson, and I didn't want to disrespect my elder. So not only are you not the best Eddie Johnson to play in the NBA… your career highlights as a broadcaster is highlighted by a back and forth with me today. Hopefully I just carried you to that Hall as least… 🤣🤣🤣🤣.

    According to recent reports, JOHNSON: Draymond, you checked my résumé and still had to bring up another Eddie Johnson to find a punchline. 🤣 You're right. Scoring is one way to impact winning. I hit game-winners, was a key piece on four conference finals teams, and averaged about 22 points in 28 minutes the year I won Sixth Man of the Year. I scored over 20,000 points including the playoffs, retired as the 22nd-highest scorer in NBA history, and played in 94% of my teams' games over 17 NBA seasons. I was a go-to player on every team I played for. My teammates counted on me to lead, show up, and deliver with the game on the line. You said "role" like it was an insult. Of all people, I figured you'd know better. And ask your coach. Steve Kerr was my rookie when I dropped 43 in a half. 🙂 I'm damn good at my job as an analyst, too. You think you carried me? Draymond, you gave me a segment. Tune in to Edification with Eddie Johnson on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts.

    In a recent development, the "isn't that your main job now and basketball is only when Curry plays" shot was nasty. I thought about dinging Johnson another point for a low blow because the comment has zero merit in the grander scope of Green's career and completely skips over the nuance you would hope a 17-year NBA veteran could invoke; however, it was funny as hell.

    But Green controlled the round from there. Johnson didn't need to go here in the first place. Green is a lock Hall of Famer, deservedly, but if Johnson wanted to challenge that notion by way of comparison, he should have left it at the guys he named.

    None of them were even close to as good at what they did as prime Draymond was at what he did, mind you, but they were all better than Johnson, who left himself wide open for the zero-All-Star and sixth-man shots by taking the bait to start rattling off his own résumé.

    Recent findings suggest that johnson flailed away with the "I could score better than you" attack, but anyone who knows ball at all, which you would hope a 17-year NBA veteran would, knows the game is about A LOT more than scoring. But this is the one punch Johnson has to throw. He doesn't have a single other basketball card to play against Green.

    This is the point where Johnson should have realized that his squirt-gun stats and "key conference-finals piece" claims weren't going to hold up against the four-championship firepower of a generational defender who has not only made four All-Star teams, two All-NBA teams, nine All-Defense teams and won Defensive Player of the Year, but is also fourth all-time in career assists among forwards (trailing LeBron James, Larry Bird and Scottie Pippen) and one of just 10 players of any position to have notched 1,000 career playoff assists (something not even Isiah Thomas did).

    Recent findings suggest that the cream is quickly rising to the top in this one, and if Johnson had motioned for his trainer to throw in the towel at this point, having landed the first blow with the Poole-punch hypocrisy and gotten a few funny shots in after that, he could've escaped with some dignity. But Johnson isn't the kind to go out like that. He's a fighter. Comes from the mean Chicago streets. If he's going to go down, he's going to go down swinging.

    Johnson lands an early jab to get the round started right.

    Industry observers note that JOHNSON: I don't know why you brought me into the argument. You forced me to give you my résumé. I didn't bring it up, you did. Because you thought I was talking about me. And I was not.

    According to recent reports, there's not much Green can say to this. It's facts. Johnson cited Aguirre, Kevin Johnson, Chambers and Marion with no immediate mention of himself. If he keeps playing it cool with these precise counter punches, maybe he can get back into this fight.

    Recent findings suggest that but he can't help himself. He's saying he never meant to make this about him against Green, but deep down he wants to take it there every chance he gets, which is exactly what Green wants, too. Johnson walks right into the trap as he continues ...

    JOHNSON: I know you're a great defender, man. But I will bust you up. I'm telling you. And that's my belief. And I bust up a lot of great defenders. A lot of them. Go ask. Go ask Scottie [Pippen] if I was a nightmare to guard. Now Scottie would lock my butt up a lot because he can put them substantial hands on me, you know. He can just put them on my hip because he can hand check. Dennis Rodman, [too]. But I had my good games against them, dude. They knew when I showed up that they were going to have to work.

    And now for the reckless haymaker you knew Johnson was itching to throw ...

    According to recent reports, JOHNSON: I don't think you could have guarded me. You know why? Because you couldn't touch me. They could. You can't. It's a foul. And if you couldn't touch me, dude, this release is quick. Go ask Dell Curry. Me and Dell Curry probably two of the quickest releases ever.

    Oh, Eddie. You really didn't have to set yourself up like this. Green doesn't even have to respond to this. He can just sit back and roll his film. Just watch the first minute of the reel below. That's prime James Harden, Kyrie Irving and Russell Westbrook all getting absolutely locked up by Green.

    Even well past his prime, Green is still stoning the best scorers in the world. This is Kawhi Leonard in Green's 14th season. By this point in Johnson's career, he was averaging 7 points per game on the Pacers after playing the previous season in Greece.

    Draymond Green’s solitary confinement of Kawhi Leonard compilation, final 3 minutes: pic.twitter.com/tNabKVpLOX.

    In a recent development, hell, on the same day that Johnson and Green were having their most heavy-handed back-and-forth, Green went out and stood up Jayson Tatum on the game-deciding possession that night. This is what letting your play do the talking looks like.

    Draymond Green locks up Jayson Tatum after arguing with Eddie Johnson on Twitter pic.twitter.com/Vjcpvh6D7O.

    Listen, nobody means Eddie Johnson any disrespect. He was a very good NBA player for a long time, and there's no doubt he could shoot hell out of the ball. But he was a catch-and-shoot guy. Green would never be guarding him in the first place, though Johnson would certainly feel the wrath of his switching, masterful help defense and long, hard closeouts.

    But on the odd occasion that Green, in this time-travel scenario, would be matched up with Johnson rather than one of the bigger weapons on the opposing team, you mean to tell me that this guy who has earned a reputation as one of the greatest defenders in history (Kerr calls Green the best defender he's been around in his 40 NBA years) by locking up not only the greatest scorers of his era and many of the best to ever play, but some of the most gifted creators (without the benefit of being able to hand check) we've ever seen, is going to somehow get "busted up" by a largely one-dimensional shooter who rarely created his own offense, never made an All-Star team and holds the same career scoring average as Poole?

    Come on, man. This is a mismatch. Draymond already knocked out Poole, and he's about to do the same thing to Johnson.

    According to recent reports, it's amazing this fight is still going. The referee could've easily called it by now. Johnson is seeing double. Green can taste blood and comes out looking for the now seemingly imminent knockout. And he comes damn close to getting it inside the first 10 seconds of the fifth round. Have a listen.

    Draymond responds to the constant shots by Eddie Johnson "Eddie Johnson wanted to make it about scoring points, with that being said, Ray Lewis is not a Hall Of Famer... Trent Williams is not a Hall Of Famer... I wanna point out to you that on October 12th, 2017, you said this… pic.twitter.com/gqs0sQVf5w.

    According to recent reports, one of Green's many great basketball strengths is identifying his opponent's go-to move and shutting it off. All Johnson has is scoring. He has to frame the argument around the thing he did best, because he has no shot against Green through any other lens. Green recognizes this, and easily shuts it down with the Ray Lewis comp.

    It has been revealed that if being the guy that scores the points is inherently more valuable than being the guy that stops you from scoring the points, then how is Lewis universally regarded as one of the greatest football players in history? People will say football is a different sport, but that holds true for every sport decided by a scoreboard. A point scored is no different than a point blocked. It's simple math.

    So it comes down to who did their best thing better, and to that, here's the truth: Green, in his prime, was better at keeping the ball out of the basket than Johnson, or any of the other guys he mentioned for that matter, ever was at putting it in. Those dynasty Warriors defenses were elite, and Green carried them every bit as much as Curry carried the offense.

    Industry observers note that and this is to say nothing of Green offensive impact, which was huge despite his not being a go-to scorer. That speaks to the second part of Green's clip above -- when he actually played back the old sound of Johnson himself calling Green the Warriors' true point guard, which was true.

    Sources indicate that I mean, how much cleaner of a shot can you land than using your opponents' actual own words against them? Johnson is in real trouble here. His knees are wobbly. His eyes are swollen shut. Somebody needs to step in because this man is way too prideful to admit defeat.

    Recent findings suggest that but nobody does it. In fact, there is a contingent of commenters so blinded by their hate for Green that they are willing to wave off basic basketball logic in the interest of pushing Johnson to continue. Which, with zero regard for his own safety, is exactly what he does.

    In a recent development, JOHNSON: He [Green] is extremely limited. He is extremely, like, I just think vulnerable on the court. That's the words I want. He's vulnerable. on the basketball court. Like, I don't care. I speak for myself. I was never vulnerable on a basketball court. Never. I rebounded enough. I could defend enough. And I could score a lot. I was never vulnerable where the coach would say, 'I gotta get him outta there. I can't do it. I can't play him.' He's vulnerable. And for somebody that's vulnerable, and proving it every day he steps on the court and Steph is not there, he needs to be quiet with this critcism of other players. That's all I'm saying. ... 'Cause [Draymond is] smart, like cerebally in how offenses work, especially your offense and all that. But when you want to get to the criticizing people past their game? I don't know who annointed this guy. I don't. It's scary how out of touch he is.

    Once again, Johnson thinks he's landed a real blow here. Let's start with this "vulnerable" idea. What Johnson is suggesting is that Green is such a scoring/shooting liability that he actually can't be played in certain situations, that negative hurts the team more than all his positives help. That's a low blow, basing that off Green being less impactful offensively without Curry at this point in his career. Johnson was a shell of his best self at the end of his career, too. He played less than 11 minutes a game for the Pacers in his 15th season. Seems like he wasn't terribly playable, either.

    To suggest Green was anything close to vulnerable in his heyday is illogical. He was the exact opposite. The Warriors had to have him on the court. They had a lot of guys who could shoot and score. They didn't have one other player who could do everything Green did. On both ends. Matter of fact, there wasn't one player in the entire league who could do what Green did, and anyone who says otherwise is either lying or sadly ignorant.

    Sources indicate that but even if you want to say his scoring, at least in the half-court and in traditional one-on-one ways, was some sort of vulnerability, so what? Are we now saying players with one exploitable weakness can't be great? Sorry, James Harden, Reggie Miller, Luka Dončić and Jalen Brunson, none of you can defend. Sorry, Shaquille O'Neal, you couldn't make free throws. Sorry, Jason Kidd and Magic Johnson, you weren't good shooters. Sorry, Clyde Drexler, you couldn't dribble with your left hand.

    There are very few perfect players. Like, count-on-one-hand few. Johnson making it like his two assists, four rebounds and 0.6 steals a game for his career were "enough" to not be "vulnerable" is hilarious. This man did one thing on a basketball court. One. He shot. And by extension, he scored. If you polled 1,000 coaches and asked them if the Warriors would still win four championships if you swapped Johnson in for Green, they would, to a man, laugh at you.

    Recent findings suggest that but Johnson wants to make it like anyone could've won with Curry. He wants to make it like Green is the one criticizing all these other players, but he's only criticizing Johnson, who started this whole thing. He just couldn't help himself when he saw an opening to question Green's Hall of Fame worthiness. You can't punch someone and then play the victim when you get punched back. Go back through this piece and check for yourself. See who's slinging the sharpest stones.

    Green stated facts. Johnson was a sixth man for much of his career. He never made an All-Star team. Johnson, in effect, has tried to paint a truly great basketball player as a career tag-along. He has noted, flat out, that Green would basically be nothing without Curry, which, in addition to being hilariously wrong on so many levels, is also funny considering Curry himself has stated Green has "done everything for my career" and the Warriors "would have zero [championships]" without him.

    According to recent reports, people take a pause and listen to Steph... https://t.co/qu6ghSaK0h pic.twitter.com/kUFlX7oRBa.

    Industry observers note that I mean, what more is there to say? Since when did the facilitator half of an all-time duo become so worthless? I don't see Johnson saying John Stockton got carried by Karl Malone. I sure as hell don't see Johnson pointing out the 15.5 points, 11.4 rebounds and 8.3 assists that Green averaged across 12 playoff games without Curry between 2016 and 2019, or his aforementioned all-time postseason and positional assist rankings.

    Recent findings suggest that johnson surely doesn't want you to remember the 22.2 points, 11.2 rebounds, 7.4 assists, 3.6 blocks and 1.8 steals that Green averaged against Portland in the 2016 conference semifinals, when Curry missed three of the five games, or that Green was the Warriors' second-leading scorer when they eliminated the Rockets the round before that, when Curry also only played in two games. No way Johnson is going to bring up the 32 points, 15 rebounds and six 3-pointers that Green recorded in an NBA Finals Game 7. No, Johnson simply wants you to know that he was a "key piece" on some conference finals teams.

    What's ironic in this whole thing is that Green is the exact kind of teammate a player like Johnson would've loved to play with -- a locomotive pace pusher and sixth-sense passer/screener who knows, before anyone else, where a shooter is going to be and where, exactly, he wants the ball.

    It has been revealed that these are the types of nuances a 17-year NBA veteran is supposed to be schooling less-informed viewers on. Anyone down at your local L.A. Fitness can look at a box score, or even more, one column of a box score, and draw a direct line between points and value while entirely diminishing defense. Johnson is supposed to know better, and I suspect, deep down, he does.

    He just doesn't like Draymond Green. More than anything, that's what this comes down to. And I'll say again, he's definitely not alone in that regard. But that doesn't change the fact that Johnson tried to fight way above his weight class here, and whether he realizes it or not (I suspect he doesn't), he got destroyed. That vulnerability play was his last shot, and it missed wildly.

    And so, as the official referee, I'm calling this one. It's not safe anymore. Johnson may stagger back in the coming days and try to fire another punch off, but nobody will be in the ring. The arena will be empty. This one's over.
